title: Year two close: the book is a person
hook: a whole Bible in order, and the Church's year; Catholics say every page points to Christ
tomorrow: Year three opens: the story after Acts

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three-year cycle and its lectio: Matthew, Mark and Luke in turn, with John in the great seasons. Your line was a, b, c. Did you find this year's letter? Today, the last day of year two. Day six hundred ninety-six.

On the evening of the first Easter, two disciples are walking from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, sixty furlongs, Luke says, of dust and disappointment. A stranger falls in beside them and asks what they're talking about. They tell him everything: the hopes, the cross, the strange report of an empty tomb. And the stranger, instead of comforting them, starts at the beginning of their own scriptures and walks them through it, Moses and the prophets, mile after mile. Later they'll say their hearts were burning. That walk is where year two ends.
screen: `THE ROAD TO EMMAUS.` → `A STRANGER WALKS BESIDE THEM.` → `MOSES AND THE PROPHETS, MILE AFTER MILE.`

segments.voice: Luke says it in one sentence. In the Douay-Rheims: "And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded to them in all the scriptures, the things that were concerning him." Catholics take that verse as the key to reading the whole Bible, and it's the road this year has walked. First, the beginning: Genesis, a garden, a flood, Abraham's tent, Joseph forgiving his brothers. Then out of Egypt: the sea, the mountain, the law. Then the kings, the prophets, the wisdom books, and the seven books found in Catholic Bibles, from Tobit to the Maccabees. Second, the Gospels: Luke's mercy, then John's signs and his Word made flesh. Third, the Church on the move: Acts, Paul's letters from Romans to Philemon, Hebrews and James, Peter, John and Jude, and the Apocalypse with its new heaven and new earth. Fourth, the year of feasts: Advent to Christ the King, and this last week, Friday, Saturday, Sunday and your own name. Saint Augustine put that reading in a pair of lines: the New Testament lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is made plain in the New. Saint Jerome, who translated the Bible into Latin, said it more sharply: not to know the scriptures is not to know Christ. That's what the carry means. For Catholics, the Bible isn't finally a book of rules or a book of history, though it holds both. It's a long way of meeting someone. And on that road, the disciples knew the stranger at last when he broke the bread. Tomorrow, year three: the story after Acts, the long history of the Church.
screen: `FROM GENESIS TO THE SEVEN BOOKS.` · `LUKE, THEN JOHN.` · `ACTS, THE LETTERS, THE APOCALYPSE.` · `THE YEAR OF FEASTS.` · then, large: `THE THINGS THAT WERE CONCERNING HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one book to keep reading. Settle, and breathe. Let this year's books pass by, not in order, just as they come: a garden, a burning bush, a psalm, a prodigal son walking home, a Samaritan woman at a well, a shipwreck, a letter, a city coming down from heaven. Notice which one tugs at you. Don't argue with it. That's the book you keep. Picture yourself opening it again next week, a few verses at a time. If you pray, you can ask to recognize him in it. The bell holds the time.
Emmaus. The village the two disciples were walking to on Easter evening, when a stranger opened the whole of scripture to them. Today's word.
Your line: the book is a person. Today, open the book you chose and read one page, slowly, the way you'd listen to someone you're getting to know. Day six hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the whole sweep of scripture read at Mass through the Church's year, and the Church encourages personal reading too, often slowly, as in lectio divina, with the Gospels at the center.

fork.setup: you're walking to Emmaus with a stranger who has explained the scriptures the whole way. it's getting dark. what do you do?
options: ask him to stay and eat with you.
run back to Jerusalem at once.
fork.reveal: they press him to stay. at table he breaks the bread, they know him, and he vanishes. then they run back to Jerusalem.

original.note: Greek: word — John's name for Christ, the Word made flesh.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Bible is a book about God.
what it means: Catholics read it as a long way of meeting a person, every page pointing to Christ.
